Eight retaining-wall pathways Start with geometry, loads, water and access; then compare systems that can answer those facts. 01 Concrete Sleeper Retaining Walls Post-and-panel systems for straight or stepped residential walls where embedment, handling access, transitions, loads and drainage are designed as one scope. 02 Segmental Block & Masonry Retaining Walls Segmental and reinforced masonry options assessed against wall geometry, footing or reinforced-soil requirements, available footprint and finish. 03 Sandstone & Natural Stone Retaining Walls For a sloping garden or failing older terrace, stone may offer a durable gravity solution when the site has sound bearing, enough footprint and safe machinery access. 04 Timber Sleeper & Garden Retaining Walls Treated timber options for appropriate lower terraces, considered alongside member durability, moisture exposure, fixings, drainage and future replacement needs. 05 Gabion Retaining Walls Rock-filled basket walls for sites where their footprint and appearance fit, with foundation, basket, stone and filter details clearly specified. 06 Retaining Wall Drainage & Excavation Coordination Planning the collection zone, separator, subsoil drain, outlet, excavation access and spoil movement that sit behind a workable wall scope. 07 Engineered & Approval-Ready Retaining Walls A coordinated information, design and certification path for walls outside simple exemptions or affected by significant loads, boundaries or nearby structures. 08 Retaining Wall Repairs & Replacement Cause-led assessment of movement, decay, washout and cracking followed by a clear repair, stabilisation or replacement scope. Read the section The wall face is not the whole level change Canberra blocks range from established inner-south gardens to recent Molonglo cut-and-fill sites. In both settings, a wall interacts with the land above it, any building or driveway load, the boundary, and water moving through or over the soil. Take one wide photograph from each end, then record the maximum retained height and the broader change in ground level. Add close views of lean, cracking, decay, washout or persistent wetness only after the overall geometry is visible. Site ledger Retaining wall Canberra: six facts to record Use these six observations to describe a new Canberra retaining wall or replacement clearly before a provider inspects the property. 01 — Grade Start the Canberra project notes with the maximum retained height, then show how this wall sits within the broader cut-and-fill relationship. 02 — Loads Nearby loads can change the Canberra project design. Photograph driveways, buildings, fences, trees, pools and other walls near the crest. 03 — Water Water can be as important as the Canberra project structure. Trace wet zones, downpipes, paved runoff and a possible lawful destination. 04 — Access Access may control the Canberra project method. Measure gates, turns, steps, overhead limits and the distance from the street. 05 — Boundaries Boundary conditions around the Canberra project need a measured record. Confirm the surveyed line, neighbouring levels, fences and shared structures. 06 — Approval path Check the Canberra project against current building-approval guidance, then examine development approval as a separate question. Separate observations from assumptions Measurements and clearly noted unknowns give a provider a reliable starting point for the Canberra project. A wet patch is evidence while its source remains a question. Movement may be visible, but buried posts or footings still need investigation. Keep the two approval checks distinct Canberra building approval and development approval use different tests. Record the Canberra project height, cut and fill, boundary position and nearby structures. An exemption under one pathway does not establish an exemption under the other. Ask for a traceable scope The written scope for the Canberra project should name the system, design roles and excavation. It should also cover spoil, drainage, outlet work, inspections and restoration. Any provisional item should identify the condition that could change the method or programme.
